> MinerU is not really a replacement for your PdfPig/markpig work. It is closer to a learned Docling/OpenDataLoader replacement: a model-heavy semantic parser that starts from rendered pages, while markpig starts from born PDF objects and deliberately preserves provenance and uncertainty.
>
> The best fit is a third optional intake/oracle lane, especially for scanned documents, tables, and the 2-D math that markpig intentionally flags rather than guesses.
>

> ### OpenDataLoader PDF > Which Mode Should I Use?
>
> ## Which Mode Should I Use?
>
> | Your Document | Mode | Install | Server Command | Client Command |
> |---------------|------|---------|----------------|----------------|
> | Standard digital PDF | Fast (default) | `pip install opendataloader-pdf` | None needed | `opendataloader-pdf file1.pdf file2.pdf folder/` |
> | Complex or nested tables | **Hybrid** | `pip install "opendataloader-pdf[hybrid]"` | `opendataloader-pdf-hybrid --port 5002` | `opendataloader-pdf --hybrid docling-fast file1.pdf file2.pdf folder/` |
> | Scanned / image-based PDF | Hybrid + OCR | `pip install "opendataloader-pdf[hybrid]"` | `opendataloader-pdf-hybrid --port 5002 --force-ocr` | `opendataloader-pdf --hybrid docling-fast file1.pdf file2.pdf folder/` |
> | Non-English scanned PDF | Hybrid + OCR | `pip install "opendataloader-pdf[hybrid]"` | `opendataloader-pdf-hybrid --port 5002 --force-ocr --ocr-lang "ko,en"` | `opendataloader-pdf --hybrid docling-fast file1.pdf file2.pdf folder/` |
> | Mathematical formulas | Hybrid + formula | `pip install "opendataloader-pdf[hy…
>
> …lder/` |
> | Charts needing description | Hybrid + picture | `pip install "opendataloader-pdf[hybrid]"` | `opendataloader-pdf-hybrid --enrich-picture-description` | `opendataloader-pdf --hybrid docling-fast --hybrid-mode full file1.pdf file2.pdf folder/` |
> | Untagged PDFs needing accessibility | Auto-tagging → Tagged PDF | `pip install opendataloader-pdf` | None needed | `opendataloader-pdf --format tagged-pdf file1.pdf file2.pdf folder/` |

> ### OpenDataLoader PDF > Advanced Features > Tagged PDF Support
>
> ### Tagged PDF Support
>
> When a PDF has structure tags, OpenDataLoader extracts the **exact layout** the author intended — no guessing, no heuristics. Headings, lists, tables, and reading order are preserved from the source.
>
> > **Output quality depends on tag quality.** Not all tagged PDFs are well-tagged. For PDFs with sparse or incorrect tags, the default heuristic mode or `--hybrid docling-fast` often produces better results.
>
> ```python
> # Batch all files in one call — each convert() spawns a JVM process, so repeated calls are slow
> opendataloader_pdf.convert(
>     input_path=["file1.pdf", "file2.pdf", "folder/"],
>     output_dir="output/",
>     use_struct_tree=True           # Use native PDF structure tags
> )
> ```
>
> Most PDF parsers ignore structure tags entirely. [Learn more](https://opendataloader.org/docs/tagged-pdf)
>
> --- [current-session | 2026-07-22 09:25 | OpenDataLoader PDF local source 5717af9:D:\aghado01\packages\opendataloader-pdf\README.md] ---
> ### OpenDataLoader PDF > PDF Accessibility & PDF/UA Conversion > Auto-Tagging
>
> ### Auto-Tagging
>
> Generate Tagged PDFs from untagged PDFs — output is a screen-reader-ready PDF with structure tags (headings, paragraphs, lists, tables, reading order).
>
> ```python
> import opendataloader_pdf
>
> # Untagged PDF in → Tagged PDF out
> opendataloader_pdf.convert(
>     input_path=["file1.pdf", "file2.pdf", "folder/"],
>     output_dir="output/",
>     format="tagged-pdf"
> )
> ```
>
> ```bash
> # CLI
> opendataloader-pdf --format tagged-pdf file1.pdf file2.pdf folder/
> ```
>
> Combine with other formats: `format="json,tagged-pdf"`.
>

>   25: public static final double DEFAULT_THRESHOLD = 0.5;
>   27: private TextSimilarity() {}
>   33: public static double similarity(String a, String b) {
>   34: if (a == null || b == null) return 0.0;
>   35: if (a.equals(b)) return 1.0;
>   36: if (a.isEmpty() || b.isEmpty()) return 0.0;
>   38: int distance = levenshteinDistance(a, b);
>   39: int maxLen = Math.max(a.length(), b.length());
>   40: return 1.0 - ((double) distance / maxLen);
>   41: }
>   46: public static boolean trustStream(String streamText, String ocrText, double threshold) {
>   47: if (streamText == null || streamText.isEmpty()) return false;
>   48: if (ocrText == null || ocrText.isEmpty()) return true;
>   49: return similarity(streamText, ocrText) >= threshold;
>   50: }
>   52: private static int levenshteinDistance(String a, String b) {
>   53: int[] prev = new int[b.length() + 1];
>   54: int[] curr = new int[b.length() + 1];
>   55: for (int j = 0; j <= b.length(); j++) prev[j] = j;
>   56: for (int i = 1; i <= a.length(); i++) {
>   57: curr[0] = i;
>   58: for (int j = 1; j <= b.length(); j++) {
>   59: int cost = a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1) ? 0 : 1;
>   60: curr[j] = Math.min(Math.min(curr[j - 1] + 1, prev[j] + 1), prev[j - 1] + cost);
>   61: }
>   62: int[] temp = prev; prev = curr; curr = temp;
>   63: }
>   64: return prev[b.length()];
>   65: }
>   66: }

> The first architectural distinction is now concrete: OpenDataLoader does not classify pages by document genre. In `auto` hybrid mode it runs the Java extractor first, then routes individual pages almost entirely on evidence of tables, CID text failure, or a large wide image. Simple pages remain deterministic Java; only selected pages are sent to the external vision backend. I’m now tracing the backend contract and the Java-side reconciliation, because that merge—not the VLM alone—is the heart of its design.

>  307: def _check_ocr_engine_available(engine_kind: str) -> tuple[bool, str]:
>  308:     """Probe runtime prerequisites for the selected OCR engine.
>  309:
>  310:     Called at startup so a missing binary or Python package surfaces before the
>  311:     first request rather than mid-conversion. Returns (ok, error_message).
>  312:
>  313:     `easyocr` ships with the `[hybrid]` extra and `auto` defers engine choice to
>  314:     docling at conversion time, so both are treated as always available. Other
>  315:     engines pull in extra system or Python dependencies that are not declared
>  316:     in pyproject and must be installed by the user.

>  388: def create_converter(
>  389:     force_full_page_ocr: bool = False,
>  390:     disable_ocr: bool = False,
>  391:     ocr_engine: str = "easyocr",
>  392:     psm: int | None = None,

>  394:     enrich_formula: bool = False,
>  395:     enrich_picture_description: bool = False,
>  396:     picture_description_prompt: str | None = None,
>  397:     device: str = "auto",
>  398: ):
>  399:     """Create a DocumentConverter with the specified options.
>  400:
>  401:     Args:
>  402:         force_full_page_ocr: If True, force OCR on all pages regardless of text content.
>  403:                             If False (default), OCR only where needed.
>  404:         disable_ocr: If True, disable OCR entirely (do_ocr=False). Useful when input PDFs
>  405:                     already have reliable embedded text — prevents duplicate text extraction
>  406:                     from images (charts, diagrams, screenshots). Mutually exclusive with
>  407:                     force_full_page_ocr at the CLI level.
>  408:         ocr_engine: OCR engine kind to use. Engine availability is delegated to docling's
>  409:                     factory (`get_ocr_factory`). Each engine has its own license, language
>  410:                     coverage, and accuracy characteristics; this project does not validate
>  411:                     engine accuracy. Default: "easyocr" (preserves prior behavior).
>  412:         psm: Tesseract Page Segmentation Mode. Only applied when ocr_engine is
>  413:              "tesseract" or "tesserocr". Ignored otherwise. Range and semantics
>  414:              are owned by Tesseract / docling; see `tesseract --help-extra`.
>  415:         ocr_lang: List of OCR language codes. The code system depends on the chosen engine
>  416:                   (EasyOCR uses 'ko,en', Tesseract uses 'kor,eng', RapidOCR uses
>  417:                   'english,chinese', ocrmac uses 'en-US'). If None, the engine's default
>  418:                   languages are used.
>  419:         enrich_formula: If True, enable formula enrichment (LaTeX extraction).
>  420:         enrich_picture_description: If True, enable picture description (alt text generation).
>  421:         picture_description_prompt: Custom prompt forwarded to the VLM. If None or blank/whitespace-only, docling's default prompt is used.
>  422:         device: Accelerator device for model inference. Options: "auto", "cpu", "cuda", "mps", "xpu".
>  423:                 "auto" lets Docling select the best available device. Default: "auto".
>  424:     """
>  425:     from docling.datamodel.accelerator_options import AcceleratorOptions
>  426:     from docling.datamodel.base_models import InputFormat
>  427:     from docling.datamodel.pipeline_options import (

>  439:     # Delegate engine selection to docling's factory. We block external plugins for

>  441:     # engines unsuitable for hybrid local mode (e.g., remote inference servers).
>  442:     ocr_factory = get_ocr_factory(allow_external_plugins=False)
>  443:     if ocr_engine in _OCR_ENGINE_DENYLIST:
>  444:         # Programmatic callers (importing this module) bypass argparse `choices`,
>  445:         # so enforce the denylist here too. Without this, the module-level claim

>  448:         available = sorted(set(ocr_factory.registered_kind) - _OCR_ENGINE_DENYLIST)
>  449:         raise ValueError(

>  451:             f"(filtered by _OCR_ENGINE_DENYLIST). Available engines: {available}"

>  473:     ):
>  474:         ocr_options.psm = psm

>  547:     }
>  548:
>  549:     /**
>  550:      * Extracts a BoundingBox from Docling bbox JSON.
>  551:      *
>  552:      * @param bboxNode   The bbox JSON node with l, t, r, b, coord_origin fields
>  553:      * @param pageIndex  The 0-indexed page number
>  554:      * @param pageHeight The page height for coordinate transformation
>  555:      * @return A BoundingBox in OpenDataLoader format
>  556:      */
>  557:     private BoundingBox extractBoundingBox(JsonNode bboxNode, int pageIndex, Double pageHeight) {
>  558:         if (bboxNode == null) {
>  559:             return new BoundingBox(pageIndex, 0, 0, 0, 0);
>  560:         }
>  561:
>  562:         double l = bboxNode.has("l") ? bboxNode.get("l").asDouble() : 0;
>  563:         double t = bboxNode.has("t") ? bboxNode.get("t").asDouble() : 0;
>  564:         double r = bboxNode.has("r") ? bboxNode.get("r").asDouble() : 0;
>  565:         double b = bboxNode.has("b") ? bboxNode.get("b").asDouble() : 0;
>  566:
>  567:         String coordOrigin = bboxNode.has("coord_origin") ?
>  568:             bboxNode.get("coord_origin").asText() : COORD_ORIGIN_BOTTOMLEFT;
>  569:
>  570:         double left, bottom, right, top;
>  571:
>  572:         if (COORD_ORIGIN_TOPLEFT.equals(coordOrigin) && pageHeight != null) {
>  573:             // Convert from TOPLEFT to BOTTOMLEFT
>  574:             // In TOPLEFT: t is distance from top, b is distance from top (t < b since t is higher)
>  575:             // In BOTTOMLEFT: bottom is distance from bottom, top is distance from bottom
>  576:             left = l;
>  577:             right = r;
>  578:             top = pageHeight - t;  // t was distance from top
>  579:             bottom = pageHeight - b;  // b was distance from top
>  580:         } else {
>  581:             // BOTTOMLEFT origin - Docling uses {l, t, r, b} where t=top, b=bottom
>  582:             left = l;
>  583:             bottom = b;
>  584:             right = r;
>  585:             top = t;
>  586:         }
>  587:
>  588:         return new BoundingBox(pageIndex, left, bottom, right, top);
>  589:     }
>  590:
>  591:     /**
>  592:      * Gets a text value from a JSON node.
>  593:      */
>  594:     private String getTextValue(JsonNode node, String fieldName) {
>  595:         if (node != null && node.has(fieldName)) {
>  596:             JsonNode field = node.get(fieldName);
>  597:             if (field.isTextual()) {
>  598:                 return field.asText();
>  599:             }
>  600:         }
>  601:         return null;
>  602:     }
>  603:
>  604:     /**
>  605:      * Sorts page contents by reading order (top to bottom, left to right).
>  606:      */
>  607:     private void sortByReadingOrder(List<IObject> contents) {
>  608:         contents.sort(new Comparator<IObject>() {
>  609:             @Override
>  610:             public int compare(IObject o1, IObject o2) {
>  611:                 // Sort by top Y (descending - higher on page first)
>  612:                 double topDiff = o2.getTopY() - o1.getTopY();
>  613:                 if (Math.abs(topDiff) > 5.0) {  // Use tolerance for same-line detection
>  614:                     return topDiff > 0 ? 1 : -1;
>  615:                 }
>  616:                 // Same line, sort by left X (ascending)
>  617:                 return Double.compare(o1.getLeftX(), o2.getLeftX());
>  618:             }
>  619:         });
>  620:     }
>  621: }

>  476: ## Frequently Asked Questions
>  478: ### What is the best PDF parser for RAG?
>  480: For RAG pipelines, you need a parser that preserves document structure, maintains correct reading order, and provides element coordinates for citations. OpenDataLoader is designed specifically for this — it outputs structured JSON with bounding boxes, handles multi-column layouts with XY-Cut++, and runs locally without GPU. In hybrid mode, it ranks #1 overall (0.907) in benchmarks.
>  482: ### What is the best open-source PDF parser?
>  486: ### How do I extract tables from PDF for LLM?
>  488: OpenDataLoader detects tables using border analysis and text clustering, preserving row/column structure. For complex tables, enable hybrid mode for +90% accuracy improvement (0.489 to 0.928 TEDS score):
>  491: # Batch all files in one call — each convert() spawns a JVM process, so repeated calls are slow
>  500: ### How does it compare to docling, marker, or pymupdf4llm?
>  504: ### Can I use this without sending data to the cloud?
>  506: Yes. OpenDataLoader runs 100% locally. No API calls, no data transmission — your documents never leave your environment. The hybrid mode backend also runs locally on your machine. Ideal for legal, healthcare, and financial documents.
>  508: ### Does it support OCR for scanned PDFs?
>  510: Yes, via hybrid mode. Install with `pip install "opendataloader-pdf[hybrid]"`, start the backend with `--force-ocr`, then process as usual. Supports multiple languages including Korean, Japanese, Chinese, Arabic, and more via `--ocr-lang`.
>  512: ### Does it work with Korean, Japanese, or Chinese documents?
>  514: Yes. For digital PDFs, text extraction works out of the box. For scanned PDFs, use hybrid mode with `--force-ocr --ocr-lang "ko,en"` (or `ja`, `ch_sim`, `ch_tra`). Coming soon: [Hancom Data Loader](https://sdk.hancom.com/en/services/1?utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=opendataloader-pdf) integration — enterprise-grade AI document analysis with built-in production-grade OCR and customer-customized models optimized for your specific document types and workflows.
>  516: ### How fast is it?
>  518: Local mode processes 60+ pages per second on CPU (0.02s/page). Hybrid mode processes 2+ pages per second (0.46s/page) with significantly higher accuracy for complex documents. No GPU required. Benchmarked on Apple M4. [Full benchmark details](https://github.com/opendataloader-project/opendataloader-bench). With multi-process batch processing, throughput exceeds 100 pages per second on 8+ core machines.
>  520: ### Does it handle multi-column layouts?
>  522: Yes. OpenDataLoader uses XY-Cut++ reading order analysis to correctly sequence text across multi-column pages, sidebars, and mixed layouts. This works in both local and hybrid modes without any configuration.
>  524: ### What is hybrid mode?
>  526: Hybrid mode combines fast local Java processing with an AI backend. Simple pages are processed locally (0.02s/page); complex pages (tables, scanned content, formulas, charts) are automatically routed to the AI backend for higher accuracy. The backend runs locally on your machine — no cloud required. See [Which Mode Should I Use?](#which-mode-should-i-use) and [Hybrid Mode Guide](https://opendataloader.org/docs/hybrid-mode).

>  555: ### Is there an automated PDF accessibility remediation tool?
>  559: ### Is this really the first open-source PDF auto-tagging tool?
>  561: Yes. Existing tools either depend on proprietary SDKs for writing structure tags, only output non-PDF formats (e.g., Docling outputs Markdown/JSON but cannot produce Tagged PDFs), or require manual intervention. OpenDataLoader is the first to do layout analysis → tag generation → Tagged PDF output entirely under an open-source license (Apache 2.0), with no proprietary dependency. Auto-tagging follows the PDF Association's Well-Tagged PDF specification and is validated using veraPDF, the industry-reference open-source PDF/A and PDF/UA validator.

>  571: ### Is OpenDataLoader PDF free?
>  573: The core library is **open-source under Apache 2.0** — free for commercial use. This includes all extraction features (text, tables, images, OCR, formulas, charts via hybrid mode), AI safety filters, Tagged PDF support, and auto-tagging to Tagged PDF. We are committed to keeping the core accessibility pipeline (layout analysis → auto-tagging → Tagged PDF) free and open-source. Enterprise add-ons (PDF/UA export, accessibility studio) are available for organizations needing end-to-end regulatory compliance.

>   16: package org.opendataloader.pdf.processors.readingorder;

>   18: import org.verapdf.wcag.algorithms.entities.IObject;

>   25: /**
>   26:  * XY-Cut++ algorithm for reading order detection based on arXiv:2504.10258.
>   27:  * <p>
>   28:  * An enhanced XY-Cut implementation that handles:
>   29:  * <ul>
>   30:  *   <li>Cross-layout elements (headers, footers spanning multiple columns)</li>
>   31:  *   <li>Adaptive axis selection based on density ratios</li>
>   32:  *   <li>L-shaped region handling</li>
>   33:  * </ul>
>   34:  * <p>
>   35:  * This is a simplified geometric implementation without semantic type priorities.
>   36:  * <p>
>   37:  * Algorithm overview:
>   38:  * <ol>
>   39:  *   <li>Pre-mask: Identify cross-layout elements (width > beta * maxWidth, overlaps >= 2)</li>
>   40:  *   <li>Compute density ratio to determine split direction preference</li>
>   41:  *   <li>Recursive segmentation with adaptive XY/YX-Cut</li>
>   42:  *   <li>Merge cross-layout elements at appropriate positions</li>
>   43:  * </ol>
>   44:  */
>   45: public class XYCutPlusPlusSorter {
>   46:
>   47:     /** Default beta multiplier for cross-layout detection threshold.
>   48:      *  Higher value = fewer elements detected as cross-layout.
>   49:      *  2.0 means element must be 2x wider than maxWidth to be considered cross-layout (effectively disabled). */
>   50:     static final double DEFAULT_BETA = 2.0;
>   51:
>   52:     /** Default density threshold for adaptive axis selection. */
>   53:     static final double DEFAULT_DENSITY_THRESHOLD = 0.9;
>   54:
>   55:     /** Minimum horizontal overlap ratio to count as overlapping. */
>   56:     static final double OVERLAP_THRESHOLD = 0.1;
>   57:
>   58:     /** Minimum number of overlaps required for cross-layout classification. */
>   59:     static final int MIN_OVERLAP_COUNT = 2;
>   60:
>   61:     /** Minimum gap size (in points) required to perform a cut.
>   62:      *  Prevents splitting on insignificant gaps (e.g., 1-pixel gaps). */
>   63:     static final double MIN_GAP_THRESHOLD = 5.0;
>   64:
>   65:     /** Width ratio threshold for narrow outlier filtering.
>   66:      *  Elements narrower than this fraction of the region width are considered
>   67:      *  potential outliers that may bridge column gaps (e.g., page numbers, footnote markers). */
>   68:     static final double NARROW_ELEMENT_WIDTH_RATIO = 0.1;
>   69:
>   70:     private XYCutPlusPlusSorter() {
>   71:         // Utility class - prevent instantiation
>   72:     }
>   73:
>   74:     // ========== PUBLIC API ==========
>   75:
>   76:     /**
>   77:      * Sort objects using XY-Cut++ algorithm with default parameters.
>   78:      *
>   79:      * @param objects List of objects to sort
>   80:      * @return Sorted list of objects in reading order
>   81:      */
>   82:     public static List<IObject> sort(List<IObject> objects) {
>   83:         return sort(objects, DEFAULT_BETA, DEFAULT_DENSITY_THRESHOLD);
>   84:     }
>   85:
>   86:     /**
>   87:      * Sort objects using XY-Cut++ algorithm with custom parameters.
>   88:      *
>   89:      * @param objects          List of objects to sort
>   90:      * @param beta             Cross-layout detection threshold multiplier
>   91:      * @param densityThreshold Density ratio threshold for axis selection
>   92:      * @return Sorted list of objects in reading order
>   93:      */
>   94:     public static List<IObject> sort(List<IObject> objects, double beta, double densityThreshold) {
>   95:         if (objects == null || objects.size() <= 1) {
>   96:             return objects;
>   97:         }
>   98:
>   99:         // Filter out objects with null bounding boxes
>  100:         List<IObject> validObjects = new ArrayList<>();
>  101:         for (IObject obj : objects) {
>  102:             if (obj != null && obj.getBoundingBox() != null) {
>  103:                 validObjects.add(obj);
>  104:             }
>  105:         }
>  106:         if (validObjects.size() <= 1) {
>  107:             return validObjects;
>  108:         }
>  109:
>  110:         // Phase 1: Pre-mask cross-layout elements
>  111:         List<IObject> crossLayoutElements = identifyCrossLayoutElements(validObjects, beta);
>  112:         List<IObject> remainingObjects = new ArrayList<>(validObjects);
>  113:         remainingObjects.removeAll(crossLayoutElements);
>  114:
>  115:         if (remainingObjects.isEmpty()) {
>  116:             // All objects are cross-layout, just sort by Y
>  117:             return sortByYThenX(validObjects);
>  118:         }
>  119:
>  120:         // Phase 2: Compute density ratio for adaptive axis selection
>  121:         double densityRatio = computeDensityRatio(remainingObjects);
>  122:         boolean preferHorizontalFirst = densityRatio > densityThreshold;
>  123:
>  124:         // Phase 3: Recursive segmentation with adaptive axis
>  125:         List<IObject> sortedMain = recursiveSegment(remainingObjects, preferHorizontalFirst);
>  126:
>  127:         // Phase 4: Merge cross-layout elements back at appropriate positions
>  128:         return mergeCrossLayoutElements(sortedMain, crossLayoutElements);
>  129:     }
>  130:
>  131:     // ========== PHASE 1: CROSS-LAYOUT DETECTION ==========
>  132:
>  133:     /**
>  134:      * Identify cross-layout elements that span multiple regions.
>  135:      * An element is cross-layout if:
>  136:      * 1. Its width exceeds beta * maxWidth (where maxWidth is the widest element)
>  137:      * 2. It horizontally overlaps with at least MIN_OVERLAP_COUNT other elements
>  138:      *
>  139:      * Using maxWidth instead of median ensures only truly wide elements
>  140:      * (like titles spanning the full page) are detected as cross-layout.
>  141:      *
>  142:      * @param objects List of objects to analyze
>  143:      * @param beta    Threshold multiplier for width comparison (e.g., 0.7 = 70% of max width)
>  144:      * @return List of cross-layout elements
>  145:      */
>  146:     static List<IObject> identifyCrossLayoutElements(List<IObject> objects, double beta) {
>  147:         List<IObject> crossLayoutElements = new ArrayList<>();
>  148:
>  149:         if (objects.size() < 3) {
>  150:             // Need at least 3 objects for meaningful cross-layout detection
>  151:             return crossLayoutElements;
>  152:         }
>  153:
>  154:         // Calculate max width among all objects
>  155:         double maxWidth = 0;
>  156:         for (IObject obj : objects) {
>  157:             BoundingBox bbox = obj.getBoundingBox();
>  158:             if (bbox != null) {
>  159:                 double width = bbox.getWidth();
>  160:                 maxWidth = Math.max(maxWidth, width);
>  161:             }
>  162:         }
>  163:
>  164:         // Threshold: element must be at least beta * maxWidth to be cross-layout
>  165:         // With beta=0.7, element must be at least 70% as wide as the widest element
>  166:         double threshold = beta * maxWidth;
>  167:
>  168:         for (IObject obj : objects) {
>  169:             BoundingBox bbox = obj.getBoundingBox();
>  170:             if (bbox == null) {
>  171:                 continue;
>  172:             }
>  173:
>  174:             double width = bbox.getWidth();

>   43: 1. The CLI is now an orchestration client
>   44:    The mineru executable does not simply call a parser. It collects files, plans tasks, starts a temporary local mineru-api service when no remote API is supplied, submits asynchronous jobs, then downloads the output archive. That orchestration begins in client.py (line 910). The real backend dispatch happens in common.py (line 668).
>   45:
>   46: The public CLI defaults to hybrid-engine; pipeline is the CPU-compatible option.
>   47:
>   48: 2. The pipeline backend is a collection of specialized models
>   49:    The pipeline initializes:
>   50:
>   51: PP-DocLayoutV2 for layout and reading order.
>   52: UniMERNet-small for formula recognition by default.
>   53: PP-FormulaNet as an optional formula recognizer.
>   54: Paddle-style OCR.
>   55: Separate classifiers/recognizers for wired and wireless tables.
>   56: Table orientation classification.
>   57: The model assembly is visible in model_init.py (line 231).
>   58:
>   59: PP-DocLayoutV2 recognizes 25 region types, including doc_title, paragraph_title, text, display_formula, inline_formula, formula_number, image, table, chart, headers, footers, references, and vertical text; see pp_doclayoutv2.py (line 33).
>   60:
>   61: The main page batch then does roughly:
>   62:
>   63: Layout detection.
>   64: Formula crop recognition.
>   65: Table orientation and wired/wireless classification.
>   66: Table OCR and HTML reconstruction.
>   67: Text OCR where needed.
>   68: Seal/vertical-text handling.
>   69: Assembly of all results into page model records.
>   70: That sequence is concentrated in batch_analyze.py (line 408).
>   71:
>   72: For born-text PDFs, MinerU does something especially relevant to your work: the layout model supplies text boxes, but the text itself is filled from PDFium/pdftext characters rather than re-recognized from pixels. See pipeline_magic_model.py (line 92) and span_pre_proc.py (line 43).
>   73:
>   74: So even its “model pipeline” is hybrid at the span-filling level:
>   75:
>   76: learned boxes + native character extraction, with OCR fallback.
>   77:
>   78: 3. The pure vlm backend parses page images
>   79:    The VLM branch renders pages and sends them to MinerU2.5-Pro-2605-1.2B. The model emits normalized blocks containing type, bbox, content, angle, and related fields. MagicModel converts those normalized coordinates back into page coordinates and constructs the common block/span representation in vlm_magic_model.py (line 29).
>   80:
>   81: Unlike the pipeline backend, the VLM supplies the content itself. That makes it more capable on visually difficult documents but also introduces the usual model hallucination and transcription risks.
>   82:
>   83: 4. The default hybrid backend combines both approaches
>   84:    Hybrid is MinerU’s most interesting branch for your purposes.
>   85:
>   86: At medium effort it:
>   87:
>   88: Runs PP-DocLayoutV2.
>   89: Uses those detected boxes as externally supplied VLM layout.
>   90: Lets the VLM interpret complex regions.
>   91: Extracts text from native PDF characters when the PDF is text-bearing.
>   92: Adds OCR-detection and formula-recognition sidecars.
>   93: Reconciles the results geometrically.
>   94: At high effort it uses the VLM’s two-step layout/extraction path instead. The control flow is in hybrid_analyze.py (line 889). Native text is restored in hybrid_magic_model.py (line 91).
>   95:
>   96: That is conceptually quite close to multi-channel consensus, except MinerU resolves the channels internally and generally emits a single answer rather than preserving disagreement as a first-class artifact.
>   97:
>   98: 5. Every backend converges on middle.json
>   99:    MinerU’s important internal contract is:
>  100:
>  101: model inference
>  102: → preproc_blocks
>  103: → para_blocks + discarded_blocks
>  104: → Markdown/content lists
>  105: middle.json keeps:
>  106:
>  107: Page size and page index.
>  108: Ordered layout/preprocessing blocks.
>  109: Paragraph blocks.
>  110: Lines and spans.
>  111: Text, inline-equation and display-equation spans.
>  112: Image/table/chart structures.
>  113: Discarded page furniture.
>  114: Bboxes and some confidence scores.
>  115: Backend and MinerU version.
>  116: The schema is described in output_files.md (line 55). MinerU itself calls middle.json the secondary-development output, while Markdown and content lists are simplified consumer formats.
>  117:
>  118: The final document pass performs:
>  119:
>  120: Formula-number attachment.
>  121: Paragraph merging.
>  122: Cross-page table merging.
>  123: Visual-caption grouping.
>  124: Optional title-level assistance.
>  125: See model_json_to_middle_json.py (line 216).
>  126:
>  127: Markdown and content lists are then rendered from the same paragraph blocks by pipeline_middle_json_mkcontent.py (line 968).
>
> === L263-305 ===
>  263: The philosophical split is fundamental:
>  264:
>  265: MinerU: render the document, let several learned models decide what the page contains, then reconcile their outputs into Markdown.
>  266: pdfdig: preserve everything the PDF actually knows, make only defensible deterministic claims, expose uncertainty explicitly, then give an LLM a small evidence-rich reconstruction problem.
>  267: That distinction matters especially for mathematics. MinerU converts precise PDF primitives into pixels and asks a recognizer to regenerate plausible LaTeX. Even when the result looks correct, it has crossed an epistemic boundary: a confidence score cannot tell you which symbol, delimiter, or index was faithfully recovered. Model errors can also compound—layout detection chooses the crop, formula detection classifies it, recognition generates LaTeX, and postprocessing normalizes the result.
>  268:
>  269: Pdfdig instead retains:
>  270:
>  271: Original glyphs and Unicode mappings.
>  272: Font identity and math/prose roles.
>  273: Baselines, sizes, advances, and orientations.
>  274: Vector rules and other path geometry.
>  275: Block and reading-order claims.
>  276: The exact reason a deterministic reconstruction became uncertain.
>  277: That supports the architecture you described:
>  278:
>  279: PDF facts
>  280: → deterministic reconstruction
>  281: → explicit confidence boundary
>  282: → compact ambiguity packet
>  283: → bounded LLM proposal
>  284: → mechanical/render gate
>  285: → audited result
>  286: The most valuable MinerU lessons are consequently procedural rather than model-related:
>  287:
>  288: Separate recognition from document assembly. Its model.json → middle.json → Markdown division reinforces pdfdig’s raw lanes → classified nodes → membrane separation.
>  289: Keep formula numbers separate until late. Detecting the number independently and only then producing \tag{...} is a concrete gap worth addressing deterministically in pdfdig.
>  290: Prevent channel interference. MinerU masks formula regions during OCR so text extraction does not duplicate or corrupt them. Pdfdig has an analogous need when allocating glyphs/rules among prose, formulas, tables, and figures.
>  291: Retain visual diagnostics. Its layout/span overlays are useful audit instruments, even though they are not evidence sources.
>  292: Process large documents in windows. That is an engineering improvement independent of its recognition strategy.
>  293: Route bad native-text documents explicitly. MinerU’s text-versus-OCR classifier illustrates useful health signals. Pdfdig can use similar signals to abstain and package a different problem—not silently switch to a model parser.
>  294: The deeper advantage of pdfdig is that the LLM receives a substantially better question. Instead of “transcribe this page image,” it can receive:
>  295:
>  296: Best-effort LaTeX.
>  297: The precise failure flags.
>  298: Glyph sequence with font, size, baseline, and bbox.
>  299: Spatial rows and fraction bars.
>  300: Relevant image crop.
>  301: Candidate grouping boundaries.
>  302: Constraints such as delimiter balance and expected render validity.
>  303: That turns the model from a stochastic transcription engine into a bounded structural reasoner. It also makes disagreement inspectable: the model’s proposal can be traced back to supplied evidence and rejected mechanically when it invents structure.
>  304:
>  305: So the useful conclusion from MinerU is almost the inverse of integration: it demonstrates how much machinery is required once raster-first learned recognition becomes the foundation. Pdfdig’s bet is that academic PDFs already contain enough latent structure to deterministically solve most of the problem—and that the unresolved remainder should be made smaller and clearer, not hidden inside another model pass.

> The code confirms a subtle but important correction to the premise: OpenDataLoader’s Java path is not VLM-led. Its default local hybrid path is Docling’s modular OCR/layout/table pipeline; the only explicit VLM in that server is optional picture-description enrichment. MinerU treats a page/image VLM as a first-class parsing route. That distinction will anchor the cross-examination.

>   43: 1. The CLI is now an orchestration client
>   44:    The mineru executable does not simply call a parser. It collects files, plans tasks, starts a temporary local mineru-api service when no remote API is supplied, submits asynchronous jobs, then downloads the output archive. That orchestration begins in client.py (line 910). The real backend dispatch happens in common.py (line 668).
>   45:
>   46: The public CLI defaults to hybrid-engine; pipeline is the CPU-compatible option.
>   47:
>   48: 2. The pipeline backend is a collection of specialized models
>   49:    The pipeline initializes:
>   50:
>   51: PP-DocLayoutV2 for layout and reading order.
>   52: UniMERNet-small for formula recognition by default.
>   53: PP-FormulaNet as an optional formula recognizer.
>   54: Paddle-style OCR.
>   55: Separate classifiers/recognizers for wired and wireless tables.
>   56: Table orientation classification.
>   57: The model assembly is visible in model_init.py (line 231).
>   58:
>   59: PP-DocLayoutV2 recognizes 25 region types, including doc_title, paragraph_title, text, display_formula, inline_formula, formula_number, image, table, chart, headers, footers, references, and vertical text; see pp_doclayoutv2.py (line 33).
>   60:
>   61: The main page batch then does roughly:
>   62:
>   63: Layout detection.
>   64: Formula crop recognition.
>   65: Table orientation and wired/wireless classification.
>   66: Table OCR and HTML reconstruction.
>   67: Text OCR where needed.
>   68: Seal/vertical-text handling.
>   69: Assembly of all results into page model records.
>   70: That sequence is concentrated in batch_analyze.py (line 408).
>   71:
>   72: For born-text PDFs, MinerU does something especially relevant to your work: the layout model supplies text boxes, but the text itself is filled from PDFium/pdftext characters rather than re-recognized from pixels. See pipeline_magic_model.py (line 92) and span_pre_proc.py (line 43).
>   73:
>   74: So even its “model pipeline” is hybrid at the span-filling level:
>   75:
>   76: learned boxes + native character extraction, with OCR fallback.
>   77:
>   78: 3. The pure vlm backend parses page images
>   79:    The VLM branch renders pages and sends them to MinerU2.5-Pro-2605-1.2B. The model emits normalized blocks containing type, bbox, content, angle, and related fields. MagicModel converts those normalized coordinates back into page coordinates and constructs the common block/span representation in vlm_magic_model.py (line 29).
>   80:
>   81: Unlike the pipeline backend, the VLM supplies the content itself. That makes it more capable on visually difficult documents but also introduces the usual model hallucination and transcription risks.
>   82:
>   83: 4. The default hybrid backend combines both approaches
>   84:    Hybrid is MinerU’s most interesting branch for your purposes.
>   85:
>   86: At medium effort it:
>   87:
>   88: Runs PP-DocLayoutV2.
>   89: Uses those detected boxes as externally supplied VLM layout.
>   90: Lets the VLM interpret complex regions.
>   91: Extracts text from native PDF characters when the PDF is text-bearing.
>   92: Adds OCR-detection and formula-recognition sidecars.
>   93: Reconciles the results geometrically.
>   94: At high effort it uses the VLM’s two-step layout/extraction path instead. The control flow is in hybrid_analyze.py (line 889). Native text is restored in hybrid_magic_model.py (line 91).
>   95:
>   96: That is conceptually quite close to multi-channel consensus, except MinerU resolves the channels internally and generally emits a single answer rather than preserving disagreement as a first-class artifact.
>   97:
>   98: 5. Every backend converges on middle.json
>   99:    MinerU’s important internal contract is:
>  100:
>  101: model inference
>  102: → preproc_blocks
>  103: → para_blocks + discarded_blocks
>  104: → Markdown/content lists
>  105: middle.json keeps:
>  106:
>  107: Page size and page index.
>  108: Ordered layout/preprocessing blocks.
>  109: Paragraph blocks.
>  110: Lines and spans.
>  111: Text, inline-equation and display-equation spans.
>  112: Image/table/chart structures.
>  113: Discarded page furniture.
>  114: Bboxes and some confidence scores.
>  115: Backend and MinerU version.
>  116: The schema is described in output_files.md (line 55). MinerU itself calls middle.json the secondary-development output, while Markdown and content lists are simplified consumer formats.
>  117:
>  118: The final document pass performs:
>  119:
>  120: Formula-number attachment.
>  121: Paragraph merging.
>  122: Cross-page table merging.
>  123: Visual-caption grouping.
>  124: Optional title-level assistance.
>  125: See model_json_to_middle_json.py (line 216).
>  126:
>  127: Markdown and content lists are then rendered from the same paragraph blocks by pipeline_middle_json_mkcontent.py (line 968).

>  110: - `Tj`, `TJ`, `'`, and `"` create text chunks.
>  234: | Priority | Signal | Backend condition | Attached “confidence” |
>  246: The values called “confidence” are fixed labels attached to rule branches. They are not calibrated posterior probabilities, are not learned from the current document, and are not used to arbitrate Java versus backend answers after inference.
>  271: **Portrait scan.** A page containing one full-page portrait scan has a large area ratio but typically a width/height ratio around 0.7–0.8, below the required 1.75. If it has no decoded text and no line objects, it falls through to Java. The Java lane can preserve the image but cannot OCR it. Therefore a normal portrait scan can require `hybrid-mode=full` even though OCR is configured as `auto`. This is a source-level inference from the conjunction in [`TriageProcessor.java:459-466`](https://github.com/opendataloader-project/opendataloader-pdf/blob/5717af950808acacebe7d2f8ac8a6a23f8aafcd0/java/opendataloader-pdf-core/src/main/java/org/opendataloader/pdf/hybrid/TriageProcessor.java#L459-L466) and the image calculation in [`TriageProcessor.java:769-803`](https://github.com/opendataloader-project/opendataloader-pdf/blob/5717af950808acacebe7d2f8ac8a6a23f8aafcd0/java/opendataloader-pdf-core/src/main/java/org/opendataloader/pdf/hybrid/TriageProcessor.java#L769-L803). The triage unit tests at this revision do not construct an `ImageChunk`, so this boundary does not appear to have a direct unit test.
>  273: **Formula page.** The Java lane has no formula recognizer, but triage has no formula signal. A born-digital formula page whose fonts decode and whose graphics do not look table-like can remain in Java. Docling formula enrichment is optional and most useful in full mode, so formula recovery is not an automatic consequence of turning hybrid mode on.
>  293: The Java and backend paths are processed sequentially even though the class-level documentation still says they run concurrently. Configuration also forces `threads=1` in hybrid mode. A `maxConcurrentRequests` setting exists and defaults to four, but at this revision its getter is not used by production processing code.
>  364: So `hybrid=on, page routed to Java` is not guaranteed to equal `hybrid=off` for that page. This is implementation drift, not a necessary property of the architecture.
>  464: | Full-page portrait scan | Likely Java under current auto rule unless another signal fires; full mode needed for reliable OCR | Visual pipeline/VLM and OCR are natural paths |
>  476: 1. **Auto triage is narrower than the backend’s advertised capability.** Portrait scans and formula pages can fail to route even though OCR/formula processing exists downstream.
>  486: 8. **Configured concurrency is not wired into production processing.** `maxConcurrentRequests` exists but has no production caller.

Completed the deep dive and cross-examination:

[OpenDataLoader PDF architecture breakdown](C:/Users/azrie/Documents/Codex/2026-07-22/lets/outputs/sol-opendataloader-pdf-breakdown.md)

Core findings:

- OpenDataLoader is a born-PDF semantic compiler: operators → native chunks → geometric/typographic heuristics → semantic graph.
- Its auto hybrid triage is primarily a Unicode-failure and table detector—not a general page-difficulty classifier.
- Backend routing is whole-page; MinerU’s hybrid architecture reconciles evidence at finer region/channel granularity.
- OpenDataLoader’s explicit local VLM is optional picture-description enrichment. MinerU makes page-image VLM parsing first-class.
- Important pressure points include portrait scans and formulas not automatically routing, Java/hybrid-Java pipeline drift, sparse-page range overprocessing, and partly dormant XY-Cut++ logic.
- The report includes the tagged-PDF lane, exact veraPDF decomposition, heuristic thresholds, backend reconciliation, IR comparison, failure modes, diagrams, and commit-pinned source links.

Both reviewed repositories remain unchanged. This was a static source trace; no live hybrid backend was run, and Maven was unavailable on the current command path.

Yeah—there really is a lot here. But rereading the retrospective makes me think your architecture is already more coherent than it feels. You’re not choosing between OpenDataLoader and MinerU; you’re defining a third decomposition.

A provisional formulation:

> A cluster-first, evidence-preserving PDF transducer that derives competing structural hypotheses from born PDF signals, resolves clear cases with deterministic witnesses and lightweight learned policies, and escalates only genuine residual ambiguity to reasoning models.

That gives the three approaches distinct centers of gravity:

| System         | Primary discovery mechanism                                | Models mainly do                                       |
| -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| OpenDataLoader | Ordered geometric and typographic heuristics               | Handle selected difficult pages                        |
| MinerU         | Learned visual segmentation and recognition                | Produce most semantic structure                        |
| Your approach  | Multi-view clustering and relational hypothesis generation | Adjudicate, route, and interpret unresolved structures |

The crucial difference is that clustering isn’t merely one table detector or preprocessing utility in your design. It discovers the document’s own regimes: body typography, heading configurations, math configurations, furniture, alignments, recurring layouts, baseline flows, and anomalous objects. That lets the document participate in defining its parser rather than being fed through one fixed universal cascade.

I’d currently picture the system as:

```text
PdfPig born evidence
    ↓
atomic and relational feature views
    ↓
multi-scale clustering / graph discovery
    ↓
small set of competing structural hypotheses
    ↓
deterministic witnesses + shallow trees/forests
    ↓
confidence boundary
    ├── accepted → measurement/manuscript IR
    └── residual → reasoning-model adjudication
```

The method families then have cleanly separated jobs:

- **Clustering discovers:** What configurations and regimes exist in this document?
- **Graphs generate relations:** Which glyphs, paths, baselines, and regions plausibly belong together?
- **Decision trees/forests score or route:** Given these candidates and witnesses, which hypothesis is supported strongly enough? Is this case anomalous?
- **Deterministic rules enforce invariants:** Impossible geometry, clear dominance, formal grammar constraints, and high-margin cases.
- **Reasoning models adjudicate residuals:** Given two or three explicit hypotheses and their evidence, which interpretation best explains the page?
- **Markpig formalizes:** Once a mathematical interpretation is accepted, turn it into a canonical AST and surface representation.

That means trees shouldn’t become a new giant parsing cascade. Their most natural uses are narrower:

- Random Forests or Extra Trees score candidate headings, captions, list structures, math groupings, or reading-order alternatives.
- Isolation Forest identifies unusual configurations that should become residuals, not decide what those configurations mean.
- A learned routing tree predicts which evidence channel or specialist should inspect a case.
- Feature importance reveals which old hand-written rules are genuinely supported and which can be removed.
- Resolved residuals become training data, gradually moving recurring cases out of the reasoning-model path.

The reasoning model also has a more precise role than “parse this page.” It receives a compact evidence packet:

```text
candidate A
candidate B
supporting and contradicting witnesses
source glyph/path IDs
local rendering
document-level analogues
requested decision
```

It should return an auditable adjudication tied back to that evidence—or decline when the evidence is insufficient. That preserves the retrospective’s most important boundary: uncertainty remains explicit and out-of-band rather than being laundered into confident Markdown.

So I think your deepest organizing principle may be:

> **Discovery before classification; competing hypotheses before adjudication; provenance before projection.**

You do not need to decide every algorithm yet. The stable architectural commitments already seem to be:

1. PdfPig evidence is never thrown away prematurely.
2. Clustering proposes structure rather than assigning final semantics.
3. Easy, high-margin decisions remain deterministic and cheap.
4. Ambiguous cases preserve multiple hypotheses.
5. Trees learn boundaries and routing policies.
6. Reasoning models operate at the residual confidence boundary.
7. Final Markdown is a projection of accepted structure, not the working memory of the parser.

That is a real architecture—not just a bag of techniques. The next useful step is probably a short “architecture charter” that names these layers and assigns ownership, before diving into another implementation subsystem.

Agreed. My previous framing was still too system-shaped. The useful unit is not “the architecture”; it is a catalog of inference problems, with an explicit account of what clustering can and cannot solve for each one.

The recurring contract should be:

| Question           | Meaning                                                               |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Population         | What objects are being clustered—glyphs, lines, blocks, paths, pages? |
| Scope              | One neighborhood, page, document, or corpus?                          |
| Feature view       | Which atomic and engineered evidence is visible?                      |
| Discovery target   | What latent grouping should clustering reveal?                        |
| Output             | Memberships, regimes, noise scores, or competing partitions?          |
| Semantic remainder | What clustering cannot name or decide?                                |

## A more concrete decomposition

| Problem                | Population                            | Clustering can discover                                       | Clustering cannot determine alone                                |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Glyphs → lines         | glyphs on a page                      | baseline and spacing groups                                   | spaces, reading direction, unusual scripts                       |
| Lines → paragraphs     | lines in a region                     | leading, indentation, alignment, and style regimes            | whether a block is prose, caption, quotation, etc.               |
| Typography regimes     | glyph runs or lines across a document | body styles, heading styles, math styles, rare configurations | semantic names for those regimes                                 |
| Columns and page zones | lines/blocks on a page                | spatial partitions and recurring alignments                   | final reading order across ambiguous partitions                  |
| Running furniture      | lines/blocks across pages             | repeated positional/textual families                          | header versus footer versus page number versus recurring content |
| Lists                  | lines and prefix configurations       | indentation and label-alignment families                      | numbered heading versus list item                                |
| Tables                 | words, rules, and paths               | x/y bands, alignment families, candidate rows and columns     | cell spans and semantic table interpretation                     |
| Math regions           | glyph/path neighborhoods              | distinct 2-D configurations, size tiers, baseline families    | final Math AST and attachment choices                            |
| Figures and captions   | images/path regions plus nearby text  | stable proximity/configuration groups                         | whether nearby prose is truly a caption                          |

This is closer to your actual breakdown: a collection of differently scoped discovery problems, not one universal clustering pass.

## Atomic versus engineered evidence

Your feature taxonomy can be made much more precise.

### 1. Born atomic features

Directly available from PdfPig:

- bbox and baseline;
- glyph advance, width, and height;
- font identity and metrics;
- font size, weight, italic state;
- fill/stroke color and rendering mode;
- character/Unicode category;
- transformation and rotation;
- path geometry;
- XObject membership;
- clipping and graphics-state information.

### 2. Local relational features

Computed between nearby atoms:

- baseline difference;
- horizontal and vertical gaps;
- overlap and containment;
- shared centers or edges;
- font/style equality;
- relative size;
- path–glyph proximity;
- local density;
- nearest-neighbor configuration;
- alignment-graph membership.

### 3. Document-relative features

These are often more useful to clustering than the raw values:

- font size divided by document body mode;
- gap divided by median leading;
- position normalized by page dimensions;
- distance from a body-style cluster;
- font/style rarity;
- indentation relative to the local column;
- deviation from the dominant baseline flow;
- whitespace separation relative to neighboring blocks.

### 4. Cross-page recurrence features

Necessary for furniture and repeated configurations:

- fraction of pages on which the configuration occurs;
- normalized-position variance;
- text-template similarity;
- digit/date-normalized text signature;
- font/style consistency;
- odd/even-page periodicity;
- run length and missing-page pattern;
- recurrence within the same page zone.

Rather than concatenate all of these into one giant feature vector, I would treat them as separate views. Geometry clustering, typography clustering, and recurrence clustering can produce independent witnesses.

## Headers: a concrete HDBSCAN + Isolation Forest decomposition

Assuming “header” means running page furniture, the observation unit should be a completed line or small line configuration—not a glyph.

A running header is not simply an anomaly. It is:

> A recurrent family of lines that is spatially stable, separated from body flow, and usually atypical relative to ordinary page content.

That distinction determines the division of labor.

### Phase 1: discover the body regimes

Run HDBSCAN over line-level flow/style features such as:

```text
font-size ratio
dominant font regime
line height
normalized width
leading above and below
left/right alignment
indent relative to column
local text density
```

This identifies one or more ordinary body regimes without assuming that the document has exactly one body style.

The useful outputs are:

- cluster membership;
- membership probability;
- HDBSCAN noise status;
- distance from the nearest body regime.

### Phase 2: score deviation from ordinary flow

Use Isolation Forest over engineered line features:

```text
normalized x/y position
distance from body regime
font/style rarity
whitespace separation
line width and density
neighbor configuration
```

Isolation Forest answers:

> How unusual is this line relative to the document’s ordinary line population?

It does **not** answer whether the line is a header. Chapter titles, captions, display equations, and isolated footnotes may also score as anomalous.

The isolation score becomes another feature or witness.

### Phase 3: find recurrence families

Take the union of:

- high-isolation lines;
- HDBSCAN noise;
- lines far from body regimes;
- optionally, lines near page extremes.

Now cluster those candidates across pages using a different feature view:

```text
normalized bbox
font/style regime
digit-normalized text signature
lexical similarity
page parity
```

HDBSCAN or hierarchical clustering with a composite/precomputed distance can discover families such as:

- the same running title on every page;
- alternating author/title headers on odd/even pages;
- page numbers with varying digits;
- repeated footer notices.

### Phase 4: classify the discovered family

The decision unit is now the recurrence family, not the individual line. Family-level features include:

```text
page coverage
longest consecutive run
odd/even periodicity
mean normalized position
position variance
style entropy
text-template similarity
median isolation score
median distance from body
whitespace separation from body
```

A shallow decision tree or Random Forest can then distinguish:

```text
running_header
running_footer
page_number
section_heading
repeated_content
unknown
```

Conceptually:

```text
line instances
    ├── HDBSCAN: ordinary flow/style regimes
    ├── Isolation Forest: deviation score
    ↓
candidate non-body lines
    ↓
cross-page HDBSCAN: recurrence families
    ↓
family-level tree: semantic role
```

The decisive header evidence is therefore not `high isolation`. It is approximately:

```text
recurrent family
+ low positional variance
+ top-page location
+ separation from body flow
+ compatible page coverage/periodicity
```

This handles several hard cases naturally:

- A chapter heading is anomalous and near the top, but usually lacks recurrence.
- Page numbers recur but have a recognizable normalized numeric template.
- Alternating running heads become two periodic families.
- A first-page omission does not destroy a density-based recurrence family.
- A repeated table heading inside the body lacks extremal position and body separation.

## The broader methodological distinction

For each subproblem, you can now ask three separate questions:

1. **Grouping:** Which observations belong together?
   - HDBSCAN, DBSCAN, hierarchical clustering, graph communities.

2. **Regime/anomaly:** Which configurations are ordinary or unusual?
   - HDBSCAN membership/noise, Isolation Forest, LOF.

3. **Role:** What does the discovered group mean?
   - family-level trees, deterministic invariants, or residual reasoning.

That separation is much less nebulous than “clustering proposes; reasoning decides.” It tells you exactly where each method enters and what object it consumes.

The next design artifact should therefore be a **clusterability matrix**, not a general architecture charter. Each row should define one problem like running headers, with:

```text
target entity
population and scope
atomic features
engineered features
clustering views
candidate-generation rule
family-level features
semantic classifier
known confounders
evaluation and ablations
```

Running headers are a good first complete row because they exercise all four evidence scales: atomic typography, local flow, document-relative anomaly, and cross-page recurrence.

> No the idea i had for isolation forest was to actually apply it to cluster labeled data in order to refine discovery along some given set of axes

Right—that is materially different. I treated Isolation Forest as an upstream anomaly filter. You mean it as a **cluster-conditioned refinement operator**:

> First discover coarse regimes with HDBSCAN. Then, within each labeled cluster, use Isolation Forest over a deliberately chosen secondary feature space to expose hidden heterogeneity along particular axes.

So the pattern is:

```text
primary feature view
    ↓
HDBSCAN
    ↓
coarse labeled clusters
    ↓
Isolation Forest within each cluster
using selected refinement axes
    ↓
cluster core + axis-specific outliers
    ↓
recluster coherent outliers / emit competing subdivision
```

The cluster label should normally define the population on which the forest is trained—not be inserted as an ordinal numeric feature.

## Why this is powerful

A cluster may be coherent in the feature space that created it but heterogeneous in another view.

For example, clustering lines on typography might produce:

```text
cluster 4:
  10 pt Times Roman
  normal weight
  similar line height
```

That cluster could contain:

- body paragraphs;
- running headers using the body font;
- footnotes;
- table cells;
- figure-source notes.

HDBSCAN has correctly discovered a typographic regime. It has not failed. You then ask whether that regime contains exceptional configurations along another set of axes:

```text
normalized page position
distance from body flow
local whitespace
line width
cross-page recurrence
neighbor configuration
```

A cluster-conditioned Isolation Forest can identify the lines that are unusual **relative to other members of the same typographic regime**. That is much more meaningful than asking whether they are globally unusual relative to every line in the document.

## Running-header example

### Primary discovery

Cluster line instances using a typography/shape feature view:

```text
font metrics
font-size ratio
weight and italic state
rendering mode
line height
character density
capitalization profile
```

Suppose HDBSCAN places ordinary body lines and same-font running headers together.

### Conditional refinement

For that particular cluster, train an Isolation Forest over structural axes:

```text
y / page height
x / page width
normalized line width
whitespace above and below
distance from the local body envelope
page-frequency of normalized text
position variance of matching text
odd/even-page recurrence
```

The forest asks:

> Which members are structurally exceptional among lines that are typographically alike?

Running headers may emerge as a small outlying subset because they combine extremal y-position, unusual separation from body flow, and cross-page recurrence.

### Coherence test

The isolated points are not immediately labeled headers. Recluster them in the refinement/recurrence space:

```text
axis outliers
    ↓
secondary HDBSCAN
    ├── stable repeated top-page family → header hypothesis
    ├── stable repeated bottom family → footer hypothesis
    ├── numeric alternating family → page-number hypothesis
    └── incoherent singleton points → residual noise
```

That final reclustering distinguishes **hidden substructure** from arbitrary anomalies.

## The resulting primitive

This gives you a reusable discovery operation:

```text
Refine(
    cluster_labels,
    conditioning_scope,
    refinement_features,
    anomaly_model,
    coherence_test
)
```

Its output is richer than revised labels:

```text
cluster core
candidate subclusters
axis-outlier memberships
anomaly margins
features responsible for separation
stability across runs
unresolved residuals
```

You could use the same operation repeatedly with different refinement views:

| Coarse cluster           | Refinement axes                    | Possible discovery                         |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| typography regime        | page position + recurrence         | headers, footers, furniture                |
| body-like lines          | indentation + prefix geometry      | lists and quotations                       |
| small-font regime        | page zone + neighbor relations     | footnotes versus captions                  |
| math-font regime         | baseline delta + size ratio        | scripts, limits, detached symbols          |
| aligned text regime      | x-bands + repeated baselines       | borderless table columns                   |
| path/glyph configuration | containment + overlap + recurrence | decorations, radicals, fraction structures |

## Important methodological consequence

Your problem breakdown may therefore be organized around **successive views of the same labeled population**, rather than a fixed sequence of semantic detectors.

For each discovery problem, specify:

1. **Primary population** — glyphs, lines, blocks, configurations.
2. **Primary clustering view** — what kind of similarity creates the coarse regime?
3. **Refinement axes** — along which orthogonal evidence could that regime hide substructure?
4. **Conditional anomaly population** — entire cluster, cluster/page intersection, or local neighborhood?
5. **Coherence test** — do the isolated members form a stable secondary cluster?
6. **Interpretation candidates** — what roles could explain the subdivision?

The key is that Isolation Forest does not merely say “this looks weird.” It says:

> Within a population already known to be alike in one respect, these members separate unusually quickly when examined along another specified set of axes.

That is a much sharper discovery mechanism—and it makes the selection of primary versus refinement feature spaces central to your actual breakdown of the PDF problem.

> i thought isolation forest was unsupervised?

Yes—Isolation Forest is unsupervised. My phrase “cluster-conditioned” did not mean using cluster labels as prediction targets.

The intended operation is:

```text
HDBSCAN(X_primary) → cluster labels

For each cluster c:
    Xc = points assigned to c
    IsolationForest.fit(X_refinement for Xc)
    → anomaly scores within c
```

The HDBSCAN label only selects the population used to fit each forest. Isolation Forest receives no target variable and does not learn “header” labels. It learns what is ordinary within that cluster along the refinement axes.

For example:

```text
HDBSCAN typography cluster:
    all 10 pt Times Roman lines

Isolation Forest fitted within that cluster on:
    normalized y-position
    whitespace separation
    recurrence
    line width
    distance from body flow
```

It may identify a small subset as unusual along those axes. Those points might form running headers—but that interpretation comes later through recurrence clustering, deterministic evidence, or another classifier.

Three related designs should be kept distinct:

1. **Cluster-conditioned Isolation Forest — unsupervised**

   Use HDBSCAN labels to partition the data, then fit an independent Isolation Forest within each partition.

2. **Cluster label included as an Isolation Forest feature — still unsupervised**

   The label becomes just another input value. This is usually less attractive because numeric cluster IDs have no meaningful ordering, and one-hot encoding mostly reproduces the partitioning less cleanly.

3. **Random Forest trained to predict HDBSCAN labels — supervised with pseudo-labels**

   Here the cluster labels are targets. This can approximate cluster boundaries, identify important features, or generalize assignments, but it is no longer Isolation Forest.

So your idea is indeed unsupervised if it is:

> HDBSCAN discovers coarse regimes; Isolation Forest examines each regime for hidden deviations along a secondary feature view.

The complete refinement operation is still something you construct around Isolation Forest:

```text
coarse cluster
→ unsupervised anomaly scores
→ candidate exceptional subset
→ test whether that subset forms coherent secondary clusters
→ retain subdivision or leave as residual
```

Isolation Forest supplies the conditional anomaly ranking. It does not itself assign the refined semantic classes.

> I think I was thinking isolation forest would help segment different types of outliers within a given cluster, which doesn't resolve their identity, but might prove useful as a clue for a reasoning agent to resolve. Take this idea across clusters, and even different clusterings, and I'm thinking about some kind of consensus or reconciliation potentially

Yes—this is substantially more precise. You’re describing **multi-view, cluster-conditioned anomaly decomposition**, followed by reconciliation.

One technical qualification: vanilla Isolation Forest produces an anomaly score, not outlier types. The segmentation appears when you retain more information than the scalar score and cluster the anomalous members by how they differ.

## Within one cluster

Suppose HDBSCAN discovers a coarse cluster \(C\). For every member, calculate:

- Isolation Forest anomaly score;
- robust residuals from the cluster center or distribution;
- per-axis anomaly contributions;
- optionally, forest path/leaf signatures.

For a typography cluster, an outlier signature might look like:

```text
position:       strongly exceptional
recurrence:     strongly exceptional
font size:      ordinary
line width:     moderately exceptional
body distance:  strongly exceptional
capitalization: ordinary
```

Another outlier in the same typography cluster might be:

```text
position:       ordinary
recurrence:     ordinary
font size:      ordinary
line width:     strongly exceptional
body distance:  moderately exceptional
capitalization: strongly exceptional
```

Both are anomalous members of the same coarse cluster, but for different reasons. Cluster those signatures and you obtain **outlier modes**:

```text
coarse cluster
    ├── core
    ├── outlier mode A: positional + recurrent
    ├── outlier mode B: width + capitalization
    └── isolated residuals with no coherent mode
```

The first mode might later support a running-header interpretation. The second might support a short heading or label interpretation. Isolation Forest has not identified either role; it has exposed structured heterogeneity.

## Useful representations for outlier segmentation

The simplest representation is often best:

```text
outlier vector =
    robust standardized residuals from its parent cluster
    + isolation score
    + membership probability
```

For example:

```text
[
  residual_y_position,
  residual_x_position,
  residual_font_size,
  residual_line_width,
  residual_whitespace_above,
  residual_recurrence,
  residual_body_distance,
  isolation_score,
  hdbscan_membership_probability
]
```

You can then HDBSCAN those outlier vectors.

More sophisticated alternatives include:

- **Per-feature Isolation Forest contributions:** which axes caused short isolation paths?
- **Forest leaf/path embeddings:** points with similar isolation behavior across trees receive similar representations.
- **Multiple typed forests:** one forest for spatial features, one for recurrence, one for typography, one for local flow. Their scores form an interpretable anomaly signature.

I particularly like the typed-forest version for your use case:

```text
anomaly signature =
[
    spatial_anomaly,
    typographic_anomaly,
    recurrence_anomaly,
    flow_anomaly,
    path_glyph_anomaly
]
```

That avoids asking one forest to make sense of every heterogeneous feature at once.

## Across different clusterings

Now repeat this over several deliberately different views of the same line population:

```text
Typography clustering
Geometry/layout clustering
Cross-page recurrence clustering
Local-flow clustering
Lexical/configuration clustering
```

Each object accumulates a witness record:

```text
line 173:
  typography:
    cluster = T4
    membership = 0.94
    spatial anomaly within T4 = 0.91

  geometry:
    cluster = G_top_margin
    membership = 0.88
    typographic anomaly within G_top_margin = 0.22

  recurrence:
    cluster = R_odd_page_title
    membership = 0.97

  flow:
    cluster = noise
    separation from body = high
```

That is much more informative than any single predicted label.

## Header example

Consider three kinds of top-page lines:

### Running header

```text
Typography view:
  ordinary member of a body-like font cluster
  strong positional/flow outlier within that cluster

Geometry view:
  stable top-page cluster

Recurrence view:
  strong repeated or odd/even family

Flow view:
  consistently detached from body flow
```

### Chapter heading

```text
Typography view:
  distinct large-font cluster

Geometry view:
  top-page or upper-body cluster

Recurrence view:
  no stable repeated family

Flow view:
  connects to the following body section
```

### Accidental top-page body line

```text
Typography view:
  body cluster

Geometry view:
  upper-page cluster

Recurrence view:
  no repeated family

Flow view:
  ordinary continuation of body flow
```

None of those views alone identifies the semantic role. Their cross-view signatures make the alternatives structurally distinguishable.

## Consensus should be evidence accumulation, not majority voting

A useful reconciliation structure is a co-association/evidence graph.

- Nodes are lines, glyph configurations, or blocks.
- Positive edges record that two objects repeatedly cluster together.
- Edge weights accumulate across views and scales.
- Negative or conflict edges record strong separation.
- Outlier-mode hyperedges record that a subset is exceptional in the same way relative to a parent regime.

Conceptually:

```text
association(i,j) =
    typographic co-membership
  + geometric co-membership
  + recurrence co-membership
  + shared anomaly mode
  + relational witnesses
  - strong separation evidence
```

Stable consensus communities become accepted structural candidates. Strongly incompatible partitions remain competing hypotheses rather than being averaged away.

This yields three outcomes:

1. **Consensus core**

   Several independent views support the same grouping.

2. **Complementary explanation**

   Different views reveal different aspects of one configuration: typography says “ordinary,” spatial refinement says “exceptional,” recurrence says “stable family.”

3. **Genuine conflict**

   Two strong views imply incompatible groupings. This is what the reasoning agent should receive.

## Reasoning-agent packet

The agent should not receive “anomaly score 0.83” in isolation. It should receive a translated evidence packet:

```text
Candidate set: lines L17, L93, L168, L241

Agreements:
- same normalized top-page position on 27/30 pages
- two alternating textual templates on odd/even pages
- same typographic regime as body text
- consistently outside the dominant baseline-flow graph

Conditional anomalies:
- spatial anomaly within typography cluster: high
- recurrence anomaly within typography cluster: high
- typographic anomaly within top-margin cluster: low

Competing interpretations:
1. alternating running header
2. repeated section label
3. body text accidentally placed in top margin

Counterevidence:
- absent on chapter-opening pages
- no continuation relation to following body blocks
```

That is excellent material for a reasoning model because the model is resolving identity from structured, contrasting evidence—not being asked to rediscover the geometry.

So the full idea is:

```text
multiple primary clusterings
    ↓
cluster-conditioned Isolation Forests
    ↓
outlier signatures
    ↓
outlier-mode clustering
    ↓
cross-view evidence graph
    ↓
consensus structures + explicit conflicts
    ↓
reasoning-agent reconciliation
```

That feels much closer to the distinctive mechanism you have in mind. It is neither OpenDataLoader’s ordered heuristic cascade nor MinerU’s learned page segmentation. It is an ensemble of unsupervised structural views that turns agreement and disagreement into explicit evidence.
